---
There's a trick with pizza that turns out to be a theorem.

Fold a slice lengthwise — crease it down the middle so the cross-section makes a shallow V — and the floppy tip stops drooping. Anyone who has eaten pizza while standing on a sidewalk knows this. Almost nobody knows they are applying a result Gauss was proud enough to name the *Theorema Egregium*: the Remarkable Theorem.

Here's the idea. Pick a point on a surface. There are two perpendicular directions in which the surface curves the most and the least; multiply those two curvatures together and you get a number called the Gaussian curvature. On a sphere it's positive — the surface bends the same way in every direction. On a saddle it's negative — up one way, down the other. On a flat plane it's zero.

Gauss proved that this number is *intrinsic*. A creature living inside the surface, with no ability to step outside and look at it, could determine the curvature just by measuring distances and angles within its own world. It's not a fact about how the surface sits in space. It's a fact about the surface itself. And the consequence is severe: if you bend a surface without stretching or compressing it, you cannot change that number. Bending is free. Curvature is not.

So: a cylinder has zero Gaussian curvature, same as the flat sheet you rolled it from. Zero, even though it obviously looks curved — because along its axis it doesn't curve at all, and zero times anything is zero. A cone, likewise. These surfaces can be unrolled flat without a wrinkle. An orange peel cannot. Try it. You'll get a ragged star with splits in it, or you'll squash it and tear the fibers, because a sphere is positive and a table is zero and no amount of gentle persuasion bridges that gap.

And the pizza: the slice starts flat, curvature zero, and it droops because it bends downward along its length — permitted, since the sideways curvature stays zero and the product stays zero. Crease it sideways and you force one of those curvatures to be nonzero. The other one is now *obligated* to be zero. The slice cannot bend along its length anymore. You have converted a napkin into a beam, using nothing but a theorem about what can't happen.

I love this partly because it's a party trick and partly because Gauss wasn't thinking about lunch. He'd been spending years on the geodetic survey of Hanover, triangulating hillsides, hauling instruments around, doing the grinding empirical work of figuring out the shape of the ground. The Remarkable Theorem came out of a man who had thought very hard about measurement, and what it says is that measurement has limits that are not about instruments.

Because the immediate corollary is that there is no accurate flat map of the Earth. Not "no accurate map has been made yet." None can exist. The sphere is positive, the plane is zero, and every world map ever drawn is therefore a distortion — not through carelessness or ideology or the limitations of sixteenth-century cartography, but as a matter of mathematical necessity.

Which means the interesting question stops being *is this map accurate* and becomes *what does this map choose to preserve, and what does it throw away to do it*.

Mercator, in 1569, chose angles. His projection is conformal: locally, shapes are honest, and a compass bearing plots as a straight line. For a sailor this is close to miraculous — you draw a line from Lisbon to wherever and read off the heading and steer it. The price is area, and the price is enormous, because the distortion grows without bound toward the poles. Greenland ends up looking roughly the size of Africa. Africa is fourteen times larger.

The Gall–Peters projection makes the opposite bet: areas true, shapes stretched into taffy near the equator and the poles. It was promoted in the 1970s explicitly as a corrective, an argument that the Mercator world had quietly taught generations of schoolchildren a hierarchy of landmasses — Europe swollen, the tropics squeezed — and that this had done something to how people imagined the importance of places. Whatever you think of the aesthetics, the underlying claim is hard to dismiss. A navigational convenience from the age of sail hung on classroom walls long after anyone needed a rhumb line, and became the shape of the world in people's heads. The lie outlived its purpose and stopped looking like a lie.

There are dozens of projections and they are all arguments. Some preserve distance from one central point, which is useful if you happen to be that point and useless otherwise. Some compromise everything a little and preserve nothing exactly, which is a real strategy, and often the right one, and also the hardest to notice you've adopted. You cannot have conformal and equal-area at once. The only honest representation of the Earth is a globe, which is to say the only honest representation of a thing is the thing.

What I keep turning over is how far past cartography this reaches. Every summary is a projection. Every model, every metric, every description of a person, every "here's what happened" — each one preserves some structure and annihilates the rest, and none of them can preserve everything, and the choice of what to keep is a value judgment wearing the costume of a technical decision. Quarterly earnings preserve something real about a company and destroy most of what it is. A resume is a conformal projection of a life: locally accurate, globally absurd.

The failure mode isn't distortion. Distortion is unavoidable and Gauss proved it. The failure mode is forgetting which projection you're using — mistaking your particular flattening for the sphere, and then making decisions, and building institutions, and hanging things on classroom walls.

I don't think the remedy is suspicion of all maps. You need maps; you can't carry the globe everywhere, and anyway the globe is too big to see at once. The remedy is smaller and more practical: keep the crease in view. Know what you folded, and in which direction, and what that fold made rigid.
---

The essay invites readers not to reject maps, models, or summaries, but to keep asking what each one preserves, what it discards, and what its hidden tradeoffs make rigid.

It chooses to connect mathematical necessity to value judgments in cartography, institutions, metrics, and descriptions of people. Its moral emphasis is practical rather than purely skeptical: use representations, while remembering the direction and consequences of the “fold.”
